items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a model describing the change from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops”.
items.answer: Demographic transition model
items.markingKey: Demographic transition model: a model describing the change from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops. [1]

items.stem: Explain why death rates fall in stage 2 of the DTM.
items.answer: Improved food supply, clean water and sanitation, medical advances (vaccination, antibiotics), better hygiene and education reduce deaths from infectious disease.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Explain why birth rates fall in stage 3.
items.answer: Falling infant mortality reduces the need for many children; urbanisation makes children costly; education and employment of women; contraception; compulsory schooling and child labour laws.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [4]

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 13 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 9 per 1000. Identify the stage of the demographic transition model. Give a reason.
items.answer: Stage 4 (low stationary): birth rate 13, death rate 9.
items.markingKey: 1 mark stage; 1 mark reason with data [2]

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 9 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 13 per 1000. (a) Calculate the rate of natural increase. (b) Suggest one economic or social problem likely in this stage and how it could be managed.
items.answer: (a) −0.4% (b) Shrinking workforce and high pension costs: pro-natalist policies, immigration, automation.
items.markingKey: (a) (9 − 13) ÷ 10 [1] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark management [2]

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 12 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 8 per 1000. (a) Describe the likely population pyramid of the country. (b) Suggest one economic or social problem likely in this stage and how it could be managed.
items.answer: (a) Narrow base, straight sides, broad top. (b) Ageing workforce: raise retirement age, encourage immigration.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark management [2]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that the demographic transition model is of little use in understanding population change in the 21st century. In your answer you may refer to policy, speed of change and migration.
items.answer: For: Based on 19th-century Europe; LICs experienced much faster death-rate decline due to imported medicine; HIV/AIDS, migration and policy are ignored; stage 5 was added later. Against: It describes the broad sequence most countries follow; useful for comparing countries and predicting needs (schools, pensions); helps explain ageing in Japan and growth in Niger. Conclusion: The DTM remains a useful descriptive framework but has limited predictive value and must be adapted to modern conditions.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “demographic transition model”?
options: Stage 1, with high and fluctuating birth and death rates and little population growth.
Stage 3, in which birth rates fall while death rates continue to fall slowly, so growth slows.
Stage 2, in which death rates fall rapidly while birth rates remain high, causing rapid growth.
A model describing the change from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops.
items.answer: A model describing the change from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops.
items.markingKey: Demographic transition model: a model describing the change from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a country develops. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “All countries must pass through all five stages of the DTM in the same order and at the same speed.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many countries passed through the stages much faster (South Korea), some have stalled, and policy has shortened stages (China).
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe how population structure changes through the stages of the DTM.
items.answer: Stage 1-2: wide base, narrow apex; stage 3: base narrows; stage 4: straight sides; stage 5: narrow base and wide top.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [3]

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 43 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 38 per 1000. Which stage of the demographic transition model is it most likely to be in?
items.answer: Stage 1

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 26 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 10 per 1000. Describe the likely population pyramid of the country.
items.answer: Narrowing base, widening middle, more elderly.

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 6 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 10 per 1000. (a) Calculate the rate of natural increase. (b) Identify the stage of the demographic transition model. Give a reason.
items.answer: (a) −0.4% (b) Stage 5 (declining (natural decrease)): birth rate 6, death rate 10.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a model based on the experience of European countries, which may not apply elsewhere”.
items.answer: Eurocentric model

items.stem: Explain why the DTM may not apply to LICs today.
items.answer: Death rates fell faster through imported medicine; birth rates may remain high for cultural or economic reasons; HIV/AIDS and conflict raise death rates; government policy changes fertility rapidly; migration is ignored.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: Explain why the transition took about 150-200 years in the UK but less than 50 years in some Asian countries.
items.answer: In the UK medical and social change was slow and home-grown; Asian countries benefited from imported technology, rapid industrialisation and urbanisation, mass education and strong family-planning policies.

items.stem: Table 11.2 gives the approximate dates when total fertility rate began to fall from high levels and when it reached replacement level (2.1): Iran: 1985-2005; Sweden: 1810-1930; Bangladesh: 1975-2015; Japan: 1920-1960. Calculate the length of the fertility transition in each country.
items.answer: Iran 20 years; Sweden 120 years; Bangladesh 40 years; Japan 40 years

items.stem: Table 11.2 gives the approximate dates when total fertility rate began to fall from high levels and when it reached replacement level (2.1): Iran: 1985-2005; Sweden: 1810-1930; Bangladesh: 1975-2015; Brazil: 1960-2005. (a) Describe the relationship between the start date and the length of the transition. (b) Suggest what this means for the usefulness of the DTM.
items.answer: (a) Countries that began later generally completed it faster. (b) The sequence holds but the timescale varies, so the DTM cannot predict timing and must be adapted for LICs.

items.stem: “The demographic transition model applies better to HICs than to LICs.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: It was based on European HICs and fits their history; HICs are now in stages 4 or 5 as predicted. Against: Even HICs show differences (USA baby boom, falling below replacement); many LICs (Bangladesh, Iran) have followed the model rapidly; others have stalled; migration matters in both. Conclusion: The model fits HICs historically, but its sequence also describes many LICs, though at a different pace and for different reasons.

items.stem: Explain how government policy can alter a country’s path through the DTM.
items.answer: Anti-natalist policies (China’s one-child policy) speed fertility decline; pro-natalist policies (France, Singapore) try to raise fertility; health spending lowers mortality.

items.stem: Table 11.2 gives the approximate dates when total fertility rate began to fall from high levels and when it reached replacement level (2.1): South Korea: 1955-1985; Bangladesh: 1975-2015; Brazil: 1960-2005; Sweden: 1810-1930. items.answer: (a) 58.8 years (b) Countries that began later generally completed it faster.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a population in which the proportion of people aged 65 and over is rising”.
items.answer: Ageing population

items.stem: Explain the economic consequences of an ageing population.
items.answer: Rising pension and health-care costs; smaller workforce and tax base; labour shortages; higher taxes or borrowing; but grey economy and older people working longer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: Explain how governments respond to an ageing population.
items.answer: Raising retirement age; encouraging private pensions; immigration of young workers; pro-natalist incentives; automation and robotics in care (Japan); promoting healthy ageing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per response [3]

items.stem: Briefly evaluate the responses to the ageing population, for Japan or another example of a country with an ageing population.
items.answer: Japan: Pension age raised towards 65-70; more women and older people in work; robots and technology in care homes; new visa schemes for foreign workers since 2019; child allowances to raise fertility (TFR about 1.2).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Named policies and their success. [5]

items.stem: Briefly describe the impacts of an ageing population, for Italy or another example of a country with an ageing population.
items.answer: Italy: About 24% aged 65+; TFR about 1.2; high pension spending (about 15% of GDP); depopulation of southern and mountain villages; reliance on migrant carers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Economic, social and spatial impacts with figures. [5]

items.stem: Explain the social consequences of a youthful population.
items.answer: Large demand for schools and teachers; youth unemployment; pressure on housing in cities; potential for unrest; but energy, innovation and future workforce.

items.stem: Assess the view that ageing populations are a greater challenge than youthful populations. In your answer you may refer to services, policy responses and jobs.
items.answer: For: Ageing raises pension and health costs while shrinking the workforce and tax base; difficult to reverse (Japan, Italy, South Korea). Against: Youthful populations need schools, health care and millions of new jobs every year; youth unemployment and unrest (Sahel); but both can be managed and both have opportunities. Conclusion: The challenges differ; ageing is harder to reverse, but youthful populations in poor countries face more immediate pressures on basic services.

items.markingKey: Early expanding stage: stage 2, in which death rates fall rapidly while birth rates remain high, causing rapid growth. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Stage 1 has no countries today.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Total population is highest at the end of the transition.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Some isolated groups may be close, but no country now has stage 1 death rates. (b) Correct. Population grows during stages 2 and 3, so it is far larger in stage 4 than in stage 1.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Total population is highest at the end of the transition.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why death rates fall in stage 2 of the DTM.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Population grows during stages 2 and 3, so it is far larger in stage 4 than in stage 1. (b) Improved food supply, clean water and sanitation, medical advances (vaccination, antibiotics), better hygiene and education reduce deaths from infectious disease.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 25 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 10 per 1000. Suggest one economic or social problem likely in this stage and how it could be managed.
items.answer: Many young adults need jobs and housing: economic development and urban planning.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark management [2]

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 6 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 14 per 1000. Describe the likely population pyramid of the country.
items.answer: Base narrower than the middle; large elderly share.

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 8 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 10 per 1000. Suggest one economic or social problem likely in this stage and how it could be managed.
items.answer: Shrinking workforce and high pension costs: pro-natalist policies, immigration, automation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark management [2]

items.stem: “The demographic transition model is of little use in understanding population change in the 21st century.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to migration, policy and stage 5.
items.answer: For: Based on 19th-century Europe; LICs experienced much faster death-rate decline due to imported medicine; HIV/AIDS, migration and policy are ignored; stage 5 was added later. Against: It describes the broad sequence most countries follow; useful for comparing countries and predicting needs (schools, pensions); helps explain ageing in Japan and growth in Niger. Conclusion: The DTM remains a useful descriptive framework but has limited predictive value and must be adapted to modern conditions.

items.stem: Country R has a crude birth rate of 8 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 11 per 1000. (a) Identify the stage of the demographic transition model. Give a reason. (b) Describe the likely population pyramid of the country.
items.answer: (a) Stage 5 (declining (natural decrease)): birth rate 8, death rate 11. (b) Base narrower than the middle; large elderly share.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark stage; 1 mark reason with data [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the change from high to low fertility, which may occur faster or slower than the model suggests”.
items.answer: Fertility transition
items.markingKey: Fertility transition: the change from high to low fertility, which may occur faster or slower than the model suggests. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “The DTM can be applied in the same way to small island states with high emigration.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why the transition took about 150-200 years in the UK but less than 50 years in some Asian countries.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Large migration flows dominate population change in places such as Samoa or Tonga. (b) In the UK medical and social change was slow and home-grown; Asian countries benefited from imported technology, rapid industrialisation and urbanisation, mass education and strong family-planning policies.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Some countries have experienced rising death rates in stage 4 or 5 because of ageing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why the DTM may not apply to LICs today.
items.answer: (a) Correct. An older population raises the crude death rate even when health care improves. (b) Death rates fell faster through imported medicine; birth rates may remain high for cultural or economic reasons; HIV/AIDS and conflict raise death rates; government policy changes fertility rapidly; migration is ignored.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: Table 11.2 gives the approximate dates when total fertility rate began to fall from high levels and when it reached replacement level (2.1): Bangladesh: 1975-2015; Brazil: 1960-2005; Iran: 1985-2005; Sweden: 1810-1930. Suggest what this means for the usefulness of the DTM.
items.answer: The sequence holds but the timescale varies, so the DTM cannot predict timing and must be adapted for LICs.

items.stem: Table 11.2 gives the approximate dates when total fertility rate began to fall from high levels and when it reached replacement level (2.1): Japan: 1920-1960; Bangladesh: 1975-2015; South Korea: 1955-1985; England and Wales: 1800-1940. (a) Calculate the length of the fertility transition in each country. (b) Calculate the mean length of the transition for these countries.
items.answer: (a) Japan 40 years; Bangladesh 40 years; South Korea 30 years; England and Wales 140 years (b) 62.5 years

items.stem: “The demographic transition model applies better to HICs than to LICs.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to migration, speed and stalled transition.
items.answer: For: It was based on European HICs and fits their history; HICs are now in stages 4 or 5 as predicted. Against: Even HICs show differences (USA baby boom, falling below replacement); many LICs (Bangladesh, Iran) have followed the model rapidly; others have stalled; migration matters in both. Conclusion: The model fits HICs historically, but its sequence also describes many LICs, though at a different pace and for different reasons.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “youthful population”?
options: The age that divides a population into two equal halves.
The spending power and economic activity of older people.
The expected funding crisis as the number of pensioners rises relative to the number of workers.
A population with a high proportion of people aged under 15.
items.answer: A population with a high proportion of people aged under 15.
items.markingKey: Youthful population: a population with a high proportion of people aged under 15. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Immigration alone can stop a population from ageing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Migrants also age; very large, continuous inflows would be needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Ageing is now happening in many middle-income countries as well as HICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the economic consequences of an ageing population.
items.answer: (a) Correct. China, Thailand and Brazil are ageing rapidly after fast fertility decline. (b) Rising pension and health-care costs; smaller workforce and tax base; labour shortages; higher taxes or borrowing; but grey economy and older people working longer.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: Table 11.3 shows the population structure (%) of Country L, with a projection for 2040: 2000: 0-14 23%, 15-64 64%, 65+ 13%. 2020: 0-14 15%, 15-64 64%, 65+ 21%. 2040: 0-14 12%, 15-64 52%, 65+ 36%. (a) Calculate the old-age dependency ratio for each year. (b) Calculate the number of people of working age per person aged 65+ in 2040. (c) Suggest why the projection for 2040 may be inaccurate.
items.answer: (a) 2000 20.3; 2020 32.8; 2040 69.2 (b) 1.44 (c) Future fertility, mortality and migration are uncertain; policy changes (immigration, pro-natalist incentives); pandemics.

items.stem: Table 11.3 shows the population structure (%) of Country K, with a projection for 2040: 2000: 0-14 17%, 15-64 66%, 65+ 17%. 2020: 0-14 20%, 15-64 61%, 65+ 19%. 2040: 0-14 11%, 15-64 54%, 65+ 35%. (a) Calculate the number of people of working age per person aged 65+ in 2040. (b) Suggest why the projection for 2040 may be inaccurate.
items.answer: (a) 1.54 (b) Future fertility, mortality and migration are uncertain; policy changes (immigration, pro-natalist incentives); pandemics.

items.stem: Table 11.3 shows the population structure (%) of Country J, with a projection for 2040: 2000: 0-14 22%, 15-64 67%, 65+ 11%. 2020: 0-14 23%, 15-64 59%, 65+ 18%. 2040: 0-14 15%, 15-64 50%, 65+ 35%. (a) Calculate the old-age dependency ratio for each year. (b) Explain two consequences of the projected change. (c) Suggest why the projection for 2040 may be inaccurate.
items.answer: (a) 2000 16.4; 2020 30.5; 2040 70 (b) Higher pension and health-care costs; fewer taxpayers per pensioner; labour shortages; greater demand for care workers; possible rise in retirement age. (c) Future fertility, mortality and migration are uncertain; policy changes (immigration, pro-natalist incentives); pandemics.
